turns.prompt_text: How do I find my body shape?
turns.response_html:
Finding your body shape is less about your weight or height and more about the proportions between your shoulders, bust, waist, and hips.

To get an accurate result, you'll need a flexible measuring tape (like the ones used for sewing).

1. Take Your Key Measurements

Stand straight with your feet together and keep the tape level around your body. It should be snug but not digging into your skin.

  • Shoulders: Have someone help you measure around the widest part of your shoulders.
  • Bust/Chest: Measure around the fullest part of your chest (across the nipples).
  • Waist: Find the narrowest part of your torso, usually an inch or two above your belly button.
  • Hips: Measure around the fullest part of your buttocks.

2. Identify Your Shape

Once you have your numbers, compare them to see which of these common categories you fall into:

ShapeKey CharacteristicComparison
RectangleStraight silhouetteShoulders, bust, and hips are within 5% of each other. Waist is not well-defined.
Pear (Triangle)Wider lower bodyHips are significantly wider (at least 5%) than your shoulders or bust.
Inverted TriangleBroader upper bodyShoulders or bust are wider than your hips.
HourglassBalanced curvesShoulders and hips are roughly equal, with a waist that is at least 25% smaller than both.
Apple (Round)Fuller midsectionBust and waist are wider than the hips; weight is carried mostly in the torso.

3. The "Mirror Trace" Method

If you don't have a measuring tape, you can use a more visual approach:

  1. Wear form-fitting clothes (like leggings or a tank top).
  2. Stand in front of a full-length mirror.
  3. Imagine (or literally trace on the mirror with a dry-erase marker) the outline from your shoulders to your hips.
  4. Look for the widest point: Is it the top? The bottom? Is there a "dip" in the middle?

Why it matters

Knowing your shape is mostly helpful for proportions in clothing. For example, "Pear" shapes often look for clothes that add volume to the shoulders to balance out the hips, while "Rectangles" might use belts to create the illusion of a narrower waist.

turns.prompt_text: My measurements are 45" shoulder, 35" bust, 30" core, 36" hips
turns.response_html:
Based on your measurements, you fall into the Inverted Triangle category.

The defining characteristic of this shape is that your top half—specifically your shoulders—is significantly broader than your lower half. In your case, your 45" shoulders are nearly 10 inches wider than your 36" hips. This creates a powerful, athletic silhouette.

Breaking Down Your Numbers

  • Shoulders (45"): This is your widest point and the dominant feature of your frame.
  • Bust (35") & Hips (36"): These are very well-balanced with one another, creating a consistent line from your chest down.
  • Core/Waist (30"): You have a natural definition here, as your waist is smaller than both your shoulders and your hips.

Styling Tips for an Inverted Triangle

The goal for many with this shape is to balance the broadness of the shoulders by adding volume or visual interest to the lower body.

  • V-Necks and Scoops: These necklines draw the eye inward and downward, which softens the horizontal line of wide shoulders.
  • A-Line Skirts & Wide-Leg Pants: Because your hips are narrower than your shoulders, styles that flare out at the bottom help create a more "Hourglass" silhouette.
  • Dark Tops, Bright Bottoms: Wearing darker colors on top and lighter or patterned colors on your lower half naturally draws focus toward your legs and balances your proportions.
  • Avoid: Boat necks (horizontal necklines) or heavy padding in the shoulders, as these will emphasize the widest part of your frame.

Finding the right interview attire for an Inverted Triangle shape is all about looking professional while ensuring your outfit doesn't feel "top-heavy." Since you're looking for Software Engineer roles, the dress code is often "business casual" or "smart casual," which gives you great flexibility.

Here are a few ways to style your proportions for a polished, confident interview look:

1. The Power of the "V" and "U"

To balance broad shoulders, avoid high, horizontal necklines (like crew necks) which can make your upper body look like a solid block.

  • The Go-To: A V-neck sweater or a button-down shirt with the top button open creates a vertical line that draws the eye toward your face rather than across your shoulders.
  • The Layer: If you wear a blazer, look for one with narrow lapels. Avoid shoulder pads, as your natural 45" shoulders already provide plenty of structure.

2. Strategic Bottoms

Since your hips (36") are narrower than your shoulders, you want to avoid "skinny" or tapered fits that can make you look unbalanced.

  • The Fit: Opt for straight-leg or athletic-taper chinos. These provide a bit more room in the thigh and a consistent silhouette from the hip down, which balances out your upper frame.
  • The Color: Try a "reverse" color palette. While many people wear dark pants and light shirts, wearing a darker navy or charcoal sweater/blazer on top with lighter grey or olive chinos on the bottom can help visually broaden your lower half.

3. Footwear Matters

It sounds small, but the weight of your shoes helps ground your look.

  • The Choice: A slightly "chunkier" shoe, like a Derby, a Chelsea boot, or a clean leather loafer, adds a bit of visual weight to your feet. This helps anchor your 45" shoulder span and makes the overall silhouette look more proportional.

Professional Presence Tips

Since you're interviewing in the Des Moines/Ankeny area, you’ll find that a "clean-cut but approachable" look works best for most local tech companies and startups.

  • Fabric Choice: Look for structured fabrics like cotton-twill or merino wool. They hold their shape well, which keeps your 30" core looking defined without the clothes sagging.
  • The "Half-Tuck": If you're wearing a button-down without a blazer, tucking it in will highlight your waist (30") and prevent the shirt from "tenting" out from your shoulders to your hips.
